summary: Net Zero & Energy Transition for ages 13–14: a capstone systems topic that ties the Weather & Climate domain together. Learners define net zero precisely (residual human-caused emissions balanced by removals, NOT zero emissions), weigh the transition as a portfolio of levers with trade-offs (renewables — often cheap, but solar and wind are intermittent and need grid/storage; electrification; energy efficiency; green hydrogen; CCS/DAC), reason quantitatively about why systemic levers dominate individual lifestyle change without concluding personal action is worthless, distinguish carbon capture and removal from solar radiation management, and engage the open ethical/governance questions around geoengineering. A policy/technology simulator makes the trade-offs modellable; a Socratic debate handles the irreducible value questions; a concept check consolidates key discriminations. Activities are agent-proposed and not independently validated against the unverified sources.
misconceptions: Thinking 'net zero' means stopping all emissions; missing that it means balancing unavoidable residual emissions with active removals.

Believing individual lifestyle changes alone can solve climate change, or the cynical opposite that individual action is pointless; the evidence-based view is that both matter but systemic/policy levers dominate the totals.
Treating one technology (all-renewables, or CCS, or hydrogen) as a single silver bullet, rather than a portfolio each with trade-offs and limits.
Confusing carbon capture (removing/storing CO2) with solar geoengineering (reflecting sunlight) — the latter cools without removing CO2, so ocean acidification and the underlying cause persist.
Assuming geoengineering is either a safe easy fix or obviously off-limits, rather than a contested, high-uncertainty option with serious governance and ethical questions and no scientific consensus.

activities.title: Planetary control desk: no single lever wins
steps: Open a climate-policy simulator with one headline number visible at the top: projected global warming by 2100.
Pull a single lever all the way to its maximum (e.g. scale renewables to 100%) and record how far the warming dial moves.

Reset, then try maximising each other single lever alone in turn — electrification of transport and heat, energy efficiency, carbon pricing, cutting methane and deforestation, ramping carbon capture and removal (CCS, DAC, afforestation) — noting the cost, scale and maturity tag attached to each.

For renewables, check the maturity/scale tag and consider what the model (or your knowledge) says is needed beyond more panels and turbines — because solar and wind are intermittent, large-scale use depends on grid upgrades and storage.
Now combine several levers at once and find a mix that actually brings projected warming toward the target, noting how each added lever shaves another slice off the gap.
Write one sentence explaining whether any single lever reached the target in this model, why or why not, and what the combination achieved that one lever could not.
activities.insight: Reaching net zero is a portfolio problem: each lever has trade-offs (cost, scale, technological maturity, side-effects) and no single 'silver bullet' suffices; in models like this the target is typically reached only when several levers are combined, each shaving part of the gap, so the reasoning must weigh trade-offs rather than crown one winner.

activities.title: Individual vs systemic: feel the arithmetic
steps: In a 'compare' mode, first max out only personal-lifestyle levers — fly less, change diet, insulate the home — and record how far the emissions/warming curve moves.
Reset and instead move the systemic levers — decarbonise the electricity grid, change industry, shift transport systems, set policy/carbon price — and record the curve's movement.
Compare the two movements side by side, reading the difference in tonnes where the tool shows it.
State in your own words where the 'big tonnes' actually come from, and whether that means personal action is pointless.
activities.insight: Both individual and systemic action are real, but the large reductions come from systemic levers (grid, industry, transport, policy); the evidence-based position avoids both 'it's all down to individuals' and the cynical 'individual action is pointless'.

activities.title: Capture vs reflect: what geoengineering does and does not fix
steps: In a clearly-flagged solar-radiation-management panel, activate fast cooling (e.g. stratospheric aerosol injection or marine cloud brightening) and watch the temperature response.
While it cools, watch the CO2 level and ocean-acidification meter — note whether they fall, stay, or keep rising.
Note any warnings the panel surfaces (e.g. regional rainfall/monsoon disruption, termination shock if deployment suddenly stops).

Separately activate a carbon capture or removal lever (CCS, DAC with storage, afforestation) and compare: which tackle CO2 itself (CCS stops new CO2 from point sources; DAC and afforestation take CO2 out of the air), and which only masks warming?
Write two sentences: one on what SRM does to temperature, one on what it does NOT fix and why that matters.
activities.insight: Solar radiation management reflects sunlight and could cool fast and relatively cheaply, but it removes no CO2 — so ocean acidification and the underlying cause persist — and it carries risks (rainfall/monsoon disruption, termination shock) and unresolved governance questions with no scientific or political consensus. This is fundamentally different from carbon capture and removal, which tackle the cause: CCS stops CO2 from point sources reaching the air, and removal methods such as DAC with storage or afforestation take CO2 out of it. Whether to deploy or research SRM is a contested value question left open here.

activities.title: Debate the climate negotiator: the questions the model cannot settle
steps: After exploring the simulator, take a role in a Socratic debate with an in-role climate negotiator or geoengineering ethicist.
Argue a position on an open question, e.g. 'Should we fund research into solar geoengineering?' or 'Is it fair to ask developing nations to skip fossil-fuelled growth?'
When the character presses you, justify your stance using what the model showed about trade-offs (cost, scale, risk, who benefits and who bears the risk).
Respond to at least one counter-argument that raises a legitimate competing viewpoint, then refine or defend your position.
Summarise which parts of your argument rest on the model's maths and which rest on values (fairness, risk tolerance, who governs).
activities.insight: Some questions in this topic — who may deploy geoengineering, how to weigh present cost against future risk, fairness between nations — are genuine value and governance questions with competing legitimate viewpoints and no purely technical answer; the model can inform them but not resolve them.

activities.title: Concept check: net-zero definitions and discriminations
steps: Decide whether 'net zero' means emitting nothing at all, or balancing residual emissions with removals — and explain the difference.

Classify each lever as mainly cutting sources or mainly increasing sinks/removals (e.g. renewables and point-source CCS cut emissions; afforestation and DAC with storage remove CO2), picturing the two sides of a net-zero balance.
Match a set of statements to 'carbon capture/removal' or 'solar radiation management', and say which one leaves ocean acidification unsolved.
Judge a claim like 'switching to electric cars makes transport zero-emission on its own' and correct it.
activities.insight: Consolidates the key discriminations: net zero ≠ zero emissions; cutting sources vs increasing sinks (the two sides of the net-zero balance); capture/removal (stops or removes CO2) vs SRM (reflects sunlight); electrification is only as clean as the grid and lifecycle behind it.

checkQuestion: A country announces it has reached 'net zero.' A student concludes 'so they've stopped emitting all greenhouse gases.' Is that what net zero means? And how is capturing CO₂ (CCS or direct air capture) different from geoengineering ideas like spraying aerosols to reflect sunlight?
checkAnswer: Net zero doesn't mean zero emissions — it means remaining ('residual') emissions are balanced by removing an equal amount of CO₂ (via sinks, CCS or direct air capture), so the NET addition is zero. Carbon capture removes and stores CO₂ (tackling the cause); solar radiation management (aerosols, cloud brightening) removes no CO₂ — it only reflects sunlight to mask warming, leaving the CO₂ and problems like ocean acidification, and carries major risks and governance challenges.
